speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: How are these negotiations different from other ones that have taken place in the past? Are there any different stipulations that could keep both sides honest?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: Well, I think there are key elements of, you know, disarming various factions, demobilizing soldiers, reconstituting a national army that reuses, really, the faction's fighters and kind of creates a space where those who were former rebel leaders are able to kind of put down their weapons and move forward towards peace. I think what is at issue is really a space where civil society, human rights activists are able to kind of continue their clamorings for peace and are able to keep all sides honest. I think this is what will hold this agreement true.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: And I think also, vigilance by the international community, to what extent -and we really don't know to what extent will the International Criminal Courts response, actually detaining or arresting one of the leaders after they may have signed a peace agreement. These are the unknowns now that will determine whether or not this agreement is lasting.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: I want to move on to Zimbabwe. The president, Robert Mugabe, just approved a new business ownership law. It requires every white-owned or foreign-owned company to hand over 51 percent - so controlling interests in their company - to indigenous Zimbabweans. If not, the government says, it's going to block any new investments, mergers or restructuring. So, first of all, how is the government defining anyone who is an indigenous Zimbabwean?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: Well, they are essentially looking to see who are there supporters three weeks before an election. Who are the supporters is a critical element in this discussion around the whole nationalizing and ownership of these assets. So on one level, we can look and say, yes, Zimbabwe is doing what many countries are doing, whether it's Russia or Venezuela, you know, trying to claim a rightful ownership over natural resources. And let's remember, there's diamond, there are tremendous mining opportunities in Zimbabwe, which is, you know, it's critical, I think, that there is resource rights asserted by countries around the world.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: But given that it is just so close to the election, Farai, it does seem like this is much more to appease those who are supporters of Zanu Piaf, the government of Robert Mugabe, to essentially say, well, if you stick with Mugabe, you get even more of the crumbs. And we know the situation in Zimbabwe with you know, historic high, 10,000 percent inflation rates with, you know, 80 percent unemployment. Clearly dangling these potential carrots could play a role in the election process.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: The devaluation of the currency in Zimbabwe has become a very bitter joke. I mean, there's all sorts of, you know, op-eds, op-ed cartoons and, you know, people riffing on how worthless the currency is. Is there still a place for international investment there in the sense that are there still people making money there?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: Well, again, let's remember Zimbabwe was once the agricultural breadbasket, and clearly the whole agricultural sector has taken a huge hit in recent years. But there are other sectors that have continued to do well, and I think that those are the sectors that will look to these carrots being dangled by Mugabe with interest.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: What do we know about the elections? What do we know about these upcoming elections in terms of there's a bit of a three-legged race with the former finance minister Simba Makoni and the long-time opposition leader, Morgan Tsvangirai. So how are these candidacies playing out in the current political context?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: Well, clearly, the political context is incredibly curtailed and constrained. So there is no freedom of the press. There is really no freedom to organize or to assemble. So it's a climate that is repressive still. And we the economic downturns, there is a sense of a real desperate situation throughout the country. So it's not an ideal moment in terms of an election. And let's remember again, there've been issues of changes of the constitution to even get to this point where Mugabe is standing.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: So it will be a hotly contested electoral process. And I think it's only telling that you know, one from Mugabe's own party has now - Makoni, Simba Makoni has now kind of split off and is presenting himself as a candidate as well. So it's going to continue to get murky, I would suspect, as the days and weeks go on before the election takes place.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Let's take a quick look at something going on in another part of the continent, China. Of course, not part of Africa, but heavily invested in Sudan, Sudanese oil. Sudan, Darfur, China is being criticized by outsiders, Westerners in particular, saying that China needs to pull back either from Sudan or use leverage to get Sudan to up its human rights standards.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Now last month, Steven Spielberg quit as artistic advisor for the games. Is that kind of an action going to really change? And when I say the games, I mean the Olympics. Is that kind of action going to change China's policy? Are we seeing any signs that China is beginning to use its leverage to force change in Sudan?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: Well, I think you're seeing a change in rhetoric, Farai. And let's be clear. There has been a clamoring of voices, civil society voices in Africa, around the world, but here in the U.S. as well. So Steven Spielberg, it's Mia Farrow. It's a bunch of people who use their own personal acclaim to draw attention to China's role in the Olympics and using the Olympics as an opportunity to bring pressure for changes in terms of Darfur and international communities, real pressure on the government of Khartoum to end the genocide and the crisis there in Darfur.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: So, you know, it's tremendous. As you've seen, this comes first from an idea from you know, professors about a month ago, about a year ago, Eric Reeves and others, professors who thought, well, let's try to see if pressure can be brought to bear on China. And from that time, a year, year and a half ago, to this point to see that at least in rhetoric, there are some changes. So what you see on this recent trip by China to Darfur is a sense of China trying to do all that, you know, at least publicly in terms of the photo ops, all that it can.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: They have brought forward engineers and teams of engineers to help with the African peacekeepers on the ground in Darfur. They have made available Chinese peacekeepers as well. But clearly, China has this critical role to play as a key trading partner and a key interest in Sudan's oil. They have a critical role to play. And these next five months before the election are going to be a critical period in which human rights activists that are concerned about Darfur, human rights activists that are concerned about Tibet and a range of other internal issues in China are going to use this platform of the Olympics to try to raise the level of pressure on China to do what it can.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Emira, thanks so much. Emira.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Co-Director, Foreign Policy and Focus, Institute for Policy Studies)
text: Oh, it's a pleasure. Thank you.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Emira Woods is co-director of Foreign Policy and Focus at the Institute for Policy Studies. She joined us from our headquarters in Washington, DC.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: Voters in Zimbabwe lined up before dawn to vote in elections that pose the biggest challenge to President Robert Mugabe in his 28 years of rule. The opposition says Mugabe is trying to steal the election, and most Western observers were barred from Zimbabwe before the vote.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: Now, the head of the Pan-African parliament charged today that they found fraudulent voter lists among other irregularities.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: You're going to hear more about this election as the results come in, and here's why: when Zimbabwe won its independence from Great Britain in 1980 and Mugabe first came to power, there was great hope for the country. But Mugabe, under the banner of populism and black sovereignty, ran the country's economy into the ground. Inflation's at a unimaginable rate of 100,000 percent.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: This in a country rich in natural resources that once exported food, tobacco and minerals.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: To get a look behind the news, we're turning to Emira Woods of the Institute for Policy Studies. She joins us from New Jersey. Thanks very much for being with us.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: It's a pleasure to be with you, Andrea.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: So, how did Robert Mugabe change and why?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: Well, to some extent he hasn't change. He has been a populist, he has run and ruled on a rhetoric of black liberation, and that has, you know, continued up through the day before the election. His last rally was very much rallying against the West, which he blames for a lot of the internal problems in Zimbabwe.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: But you would say, you know, beyond that what has changed over these years is that the liberation leader that many respected and applauded really became very much over the 28-year period a dictator that closed off the political space that did not allow newspapers to operate freely, clamp down on journalists of all kinds and had brutal crackdowns on oppositions, most notably over the last year and a half preceding the election.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: And what were the decisions he made about the economy that have so devastated the country?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: Well, the economy, I think, you have to look to two causes - one internal and one external. Internally there was this push to push forward land reform and changes in land ownership. Now, remember, Rhodesia, which was the name of the country before it became Zimbabwe, before independence, was white ruled. So a key part of Mugabe's rule was to equalize, to get rid of the white rule essentially.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: And there was a real dominance of whites in land ownership, especially in the farming, the core agricultural sector of the Zimbabwean economy. Now, the problem is that much of the redistribution went to Mugabe cronies and did not really push forward a way to manage the agricultural sector in ways that were sustainable.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: Now, the external piece of that is also important. The sanctions in place now for almost 10 years on Zimbabwe have also had an impact on the economy. So, whether it's the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund or bilateral donors - the U.S. and U.K. in particular - there have been sanctions that have had economic implications there on Zimbabwe.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: Now, this has happened at a time that other countries in sub-Saharan Africa seem to finally moving toward true democracy. Do you see examples of that? Tell me about them.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: Clearly. I mean, so, the most enlightened and the most upheld is South Africa, which ended the racist white rule of the apartheid regime back in 1994. And throughout the region you have extraordinary leaps forward when it comes to democracy.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: Clearly Botswana, one of the neighbors in the southern Africa region with Zimbabwe, has been a democracy now since independence. And you have Botswana being held up as a beacon of democracy, not only for Africa but for much of the world.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: You also have Mozambique having come through years of conflict emerging with a woman prime minister and some extraordinary achievements in terms of women's leadership. So, there's a lot happening on the continent or even in that sub-region when it comes to an open political space, when it comes to freedom of the press, when it comes to these core building blocks of democracy. And I think it bodes well for all of Africa.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: So, Emira Woods, what are you predictions both for today's elections and, more importantly, for Zimbabwe's future?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: Well, we don't know the outcome of this election will be. To be honest there is quite a record of elections that have been stolen in Zimbabwe. And I think the worry is that the outbreak of violence after the stolen elections in Kenya could well be repeated in Zimbabwe. That is the fear that many have. I think the hope is that the will of the people for change will be expected and that rule of law and a process towards real economic stability can be put forward in a way that people can have meaningful lives again in their country.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: Emira Woods is the co-director of Foreign Policy in Focus at the Institute for Policy Studies. She joined us from New Jersey. Thank you very much for speaking with us.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute for Police Studies)
text: It's a pleasure. Thank you, Andrea.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: Next up on ALL THINGS CONSIDERED, the tale of an underdog. March Madness and magic.

speaker_label: ANDREA SEABROOK, host
text: It's ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Now we've got more on the Zimbabwean elections and news from Somalia with Emira Woods; she is the co-director of foreign policy and focus at the Institute for Policy Studies. Emira, great to have you on again.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: It's a joy to be with you.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: So you just heard Imani Countess talk about the posting of election results in each ward. But who's really responsible for counting the votes?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: Well, technically it is that Zimbabwe Elections Commission and they are coming together in one central place. This was hotly debated. You know, they are collecting data from all around the country and tallying it in one central place, in spite of the fact that each individual polling place - and there were, you know, again, all over the country, these polling places were able to post the results as of Saturday. But yet somehow the electoral commission wants to have this central collection and tallying to be able to put out what they say the official results of this election. They are the only ones vested with that capacity, with that responsibility.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: I've talked to people in Zimbabwe, and you know, just everyday folks, and they are all on pins and needles awaiting the results. Some people say uh-oh the vote's going to be hijacked. Other people are like, you know, perhaps if Mugabe loses he's going to try to get out of the country and build a feather nest somewhere else. What's going on? When can we actually expect the results and is there a chance they'll be tampered with?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: Well, we just don't know. I mean honestly, as of this moment I think there are two-thirds of the vote on the parliamentary results that have been tallied and officially announced. And it is very close from that of this moment, I think there are two-thirds of the vote on the parliamentary results that have been tallied and officially announced, and it is very close from that official announcement between MDC, the Movement for Democratic Change, and ZANU-PF, the ruling party's candidates in the parliament. MDC is slightly ahead in those official results, but they are really neck and neck, according to these most-recent reports, with two-thirds of the counting in.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: But on the presidential election side, we really don't have any official announcement three days after the election, you know, and it is appalling, really, that it is taking so long for the results on the presidential election to be announced.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: Now, there have been - you know, again, it's unconfirmed reports, but the Movement for Democratic Change says that they feel they have actually won the majority, and there are reports on BBC and elsewhere that they may have up to 48 percent of the vote. Some say it's slightly higher. They may not have the 51 percent needed to avoid a run-off, but that is all unclear.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: The longer this process goes without an official announcement coming from the ZEC, the Zimbabwean Electoral Commission, it is really appalling, and you have more and more pronouncements.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: You know, the Pan-African Parliament, which was there as an observer mission, one of the few international observer missions in Zimbabwe for the elections, their official observer said, look, what is happening? The results were pretty much known days ago, and yet delay after delay on these announcements, it's creating such uncertainty.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: And you know, I'm here in Maryland, Farai, and we had one district in Maryland on election night; because there was a snowstorm the results weren't announced until the next day, and we were all on pins and needles for just a couple hours.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Right.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: That was the Donna Edwards candidacy here in Maryland. But can you imagine waiting three, four days, you know, as it seems like we're heading towards now without knowing the results of an election?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: That is so critical, particularly in an environment where there is such a demand for change, in an environment where people left their various places of exile from South Africa, from Mozambique, from all around the region, to take that courageous and costly stance to go home and vote...

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Emira, let me jump in because the Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice is actually worried that there hasn't been enough election monitoring, and here's what she said.

speaker_label: Secretary CONDOLEEZZA RICE (U.S. State Department)
text: We've made very clear our concerns about how this election might be conducted, given the very bad record of Mugabe concerning his people, the opposition, the region, and we've tried to make a case, as has the entire world, that there needed to be free and fair elections in Zimbabwe as much as it was possible.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Now, the U.S. has made - has not been shy about calling Mugabe and Zimbabwe kind of rogue and outside of the interests of the U.S. What do you think the U.S. has at stake in this election?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: Well, clearly when it comes to Africa the U.S. is interested in Africa's resources. That is clear regardless of what the country. And we have to remember, Zimbabwe does have mining interests that are very much relevant and very much at play. But I think there is a more subtle issue here, where you know, Mugabe has actually been able to get on his bully pulpit and rise up, you know, speaking out against the U.S. and the former colonizers, the U.K. For him it is these external hands that have created the economic crisis that is currently in Zimbabwe, and you know, discussions in the U.S. State Department using the term regime change after that term was actually placed on Iraq.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: We saw what happened in the case of Iraq. Regime change has led to disaster. Now when people hear regime change coming out of the State Department, there's a lot of worry about manipulation of processes, and so there is concern that the U.S. may not be playing fair, that there may be back-handed deals in which certain organizations are supported by the U.S., and these actually contribute to a climate of anxiety, where the U.S. and the U.K., even if they may be saying absolutely the right thing in this context, are not seen as really honest brokers.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Let's take a quick tour of what's going on in Somalia. You've got insurgents continuing to battle the Somali government, and the United Nations Security Council is considering if it should send more than 25,000 peacekeepers to Somalia to replace the stretched African Union force.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Now, briefly, what are the negotiations going on around that?

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: Well, let's remember, Farai, Somalia is a country that was without a government for 15 years. Finally in June, 2006, a government came to power. It was called the Union of Islamic Courts, and from June, 2006 to December, 2006, they were able to maintain governance in Somalia, and they were able to maintain peace and stability.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: People could send their children to school, women could walk the streets, and yet the U.S., again, the heavy hand of the U.S., deciding that, well, the Union of Islamic Courts had Islamic in their name and they must be extremists.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: And so the U.S. started aerial bombardment from December '06 until - really about a month ago we were hearing reports of U.S. bombardments in Somalia, creating instability in the country that has really continued till this day.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: So you have almost daily reports of skirmishes, of fights, and the report this week was of a battle, really, between the former forces of this Union of Islamic States and these Ethiopian troops that are really seen as a proxy for the U.S. there in Somalia.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: So what is happening is you have innocent civilians being caught in the middle, and there is tremendous discussion and debate going on within the U.N. at the security council level, also within the African Union, as to how can peace be returned to Somalia again.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: So there are a number of efforts under way to put forward, for example, a resolution that neighboring states, particularly Ethiopia, should not have troops permanently stationed, ending the occupation of Ethiopia. Ethiopian troops in Somalia is a core part of bringing the voice of the Somali people, peace and stability to Somalia, again.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: So there are negotiations underway as to how can we end, how can the international community play a role to bring an end to the violence that has so crippled Somalia in the last year and a half, and how do you withdraw not only the Ethiopian forces but also the U.S. attacks that have had such detrimental impacts on civilians.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Well, Emira, we're going to have to leave it there for today. Thanks again.

speaker_label: Ms. EMIRA WOODS (Institute of Policy Studies)
text: A pleasure. Thank you, Farai.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Emira Woods is co-director of Foreign Policy in Focus at the Institute for Policy Studies, and she joined us from our headquarters in Washington, D.C.
